title: Microsoft Excel Basics (Canada)
summary: By the end, learners can open a blank workbook, enter text and numbers in cells, apply simple formatting, write a basic formula that starts with an equal sign, use AutoSum, and save or print their work.

lessons.title: What is Excel?
lessons.html:
Microsoft Excel is a program for lists and numbers. Microsoft’s basic-tasks guide says Excel works well for simple calculations and for tracking many kinds of information. The key is a grid of cells. Cells can hold numbers, text, or formulas (instructions that calculate). You group cells in rows and columns so you can add, sort, filter, and later make charts if you want to.

Excel files are called workbooks. Each workbook has one or more sheets (also called spreadsheets). You can add more sheets, or start a new workbook when you want to keep information separate.

To start a blank workbook (Microsoft’s steps):

  1. Click File, then New.
  2. Under New, click Blank workbook.

Each cell has an address made from its column letter and row number. Cell A1 is column A, row 1 — the top-left cell on a new sheet.

People in Canada use spreadsheets for many everyday jobs: hours worked, a small expense list, a class attendance sheet, or a farm or household inventory. This course uses Canadian spelling and simple examples. It will not tell you how to file taxes or choose a bookkeeping system.

If Excel is not on the computer in front of you, ask your adult learning council which version they have, or whether you can use Excel for the web with a sign-in they approve. Do not buy software because this lesson mentioned it.

lessons.title: Enter data in cells
lessons.html:
Entering data means typing information into cells so Excel can use it later.

Microsoft’s steps:

  1. Click an empty cell. On a new sheet, try A1.
  2. Type text or a number.
  3. Press Enter or Tab to move to the next cell.

Enter usually moves you down to the cell below. Tab usually moves you right to the next column. If you make a mistake, click the cell again and type the correction, or edit what you see.

A simple practice table (sample data only):

AB
1ItemAmount
2Fuel80
3Feed45
4Supplies25

Type the words in column A and the numbers in column B. Keep one kind of information in each column. That makes adding and sorting easier later.

Tips:

  • Click once to select a cell before you type.
  • If you start typing in the wrong cell, click the cell again and type the correction.
  • Do not type a space after a number if you want Excel to treat it as a number.
  • Use sample amounts in this course. Do not enter real banking passwords or anyone’s private pay details into a shared computer.

When a cell is selected, you can also see and edit its contents in the formula bar near the top of the window (you will use this more in Lesson 4).

lessons.title: Make a sheet easier to read
lessons.html:
Plain numbers are useful. A little formatting makes a sheet easier to scan.

Borders (Microsoft):

  1. Select the cell or range you want to outline.
  2. On the Home tab, in the Font group, click the arrow next to Borders, and choose a style.

Shading (fill colour):

  1. Select the cells.
  2. On the Home tab, in the Font group, click the arrow next to Fill Color, and pick a colour.

Use light colours for titles so the text stays readable.

Number formats: Microsoft says you can add a format such as currency, percentages, or dates so different kinds of numbers are easier to tell apart.

  1. Select the cells that have numbers.
  2. Click the Home tab, then the arrow in the General box.
  3. Pick a number format. If you do not see the one you want, click More Number Formats.

Choose a format that matches how you write money or dates in Canada. If you are not sure which currency or date style to pick, ask a tutor. This course does not tell you which format a workplace or the CRA requires.

You can also select a block of cells by clicking the first cell and dragging to the last cell. Microsoft notes you can hold Shift and use the arrow keys to select with the keyboard.

Save your work after you format (Lesson 5) so you do not lose the layout.

lessons.title: Simple formulas and AutoSum
lessons.html:
A formula tells Excel to calculate. Microsoft says a simple formula always starts with an equal sign (=). Then you type numbers and operators:

  • plus + to add
  • minus - to subtract
  • asterisk * to multiply
  • forward slash / to divide

Examples from Microsoft: =2+4, =4-2, =2*4, or =4/2. Click a cell, type the formula, then press Enter (Windows) or Return (Mac). You can also point at cells instead of typing the numbers: for example, =B2+B3+B4.

Microsoft notes that multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. So =5+2*3 multiplies 2 and 3 first, then adds 5.

AutoSum is a fast way to add a column or row. Microsoft’s steps:

  1. Select the cell immediately below a column of numbers, or immediately to the right of a row of numbers.
  2. On the Home tab (or the Formulas tab), click AutoSum.
  3. Press Enter.

AutoSum inserts a SUM function for you. You can also type a SUM formula yourself, such as =SUM(B2:B4), which adds the cells from B2 through B4.

If a formula does not look right, click the cell and check the formula bar at the top. Fix the equal sign and cell addresses, then press Enter again.

Practise on the sample amounts from Lesson 2. This is not payroll or tax calculation advice.

lessons.title: Save and print your workbook
lessons.html:
Saving puts your workbook in a file so you can close Excel without losing the work.

Microsoft’s basic steps:

  1. Click the Save button on the Quick Access Toolbar, or press Ctrl+S. If you have saved this file before, you are done.
  2. The first time, choose Save As, pick a location, browse to a folder, type a name in the File name box, and click Save.

A clear name helps you find the file later, such as hours-november or expense-list-practice. Save it in a folder you know, such as Documents (see the Everyday Computers course for File Explorer).

Save often while you work. Microsoft also describes AutoRecovery, which can keep a backup if something goes wrong, such as a power cut. AutoRecovery is not the same as you saving the file yourself, so do not rely on it alone.

To print (Microsoft):

  1. Click File, then Print, or press Ctrl+P.
  2. Preview the pages with the Next Page and Previous Page arrows.
  3. If the layout looks wrong, you can change margins or page breaks.
  4. Click Print.

Preview first so you do not waste paper. If you are on a shared learning-centre printer, ask staff which printer to pick.

When you finish, close the file. You can open it later from File Explorer or from File > Open in Excel.
